answer: A commercial bank must also take into account other UNSCRs and lists in the first and fourth schedules of UAPA, 1967, along with any amendments to these lists [S2].

The commercial bank shall ensure adherence to the provisions of Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, and Rules made thereunder [S1]. Furthermore, the bank must ensure meticulous compliance with any instructions or communications on this matter issued by the RBI based on advice from the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India [S1].
The bank shall review its risk assessment at least annually [S1].

The bank shall temporarily cease operations in the account until the customer submits the PAN or equivalent e-documents thereof or Form No. 60 [S1]. Before temporarily ceasing operations, the bank must give the customer an accessible notice and a reasonable opportunity to be heard [S1].

The 'at par' cheque facility offered by the bank to co-operative banks shall be monitored and such arrangements reviewed to assess risks including credit risk and reputational risk [S4]. The bank shall also retain the right to verify the records maintained by the customer cooperative banks/societies for compliance with extant instructions on KYC and AML under such arrangements [S4].

Any remittance of funds by way of demand draft, mail/telegraphic transfer/NEFT/IMPS or any other mode and issue of travellers’ cheques for a value of ₹50,000 and above shall be effected by debit to the customer’s account or against cheques and not against cash payment [S1].

A commercial bank shall consider the FATF Statements circulated by the RBI from time to time, and publicly available information, for identifying countries that do not or insufficiently apply the FATF Recommendations [S1].
The bank shall not collect account payee cheques for any person other than the payee constituent [S1].

The bank shall undertake countermeasures when called upon so to do by any international or intergovernmental organisation of which India is a member and which is accepted by the Central Government [S1].

The RBI's KYC requirements do not replace obligations under other laws and regulations; rather, they are in addition to them [S2]. For commercial banks, a bank shall continue to carry out customer due diligence processes in line with regulations governing KYC, AML, CFT, and PMLA, 2002, in addition to ensuring compliance with FEMA for overseas remittances [S1].

Yes, a commercial bank may undertake V-CIP to carry out CDD in case of new customer onboarding for individual customers and Beneficial Owners (BOs) in case of Legal Entity (LE) customers [S1]. This is listed under point (1) of paragraph 26 [S1].

The bank shall adopt a risk-based approach for periodic updation of KYC to keep the information or data collected under CDD up-to-date and relevant, especially for high-risk customers [S2]. Specifically, periodic updation must occur at least every two years for high-risk customers, every eight years for medium risk customers, and every 10 years for low-risk customers from the account opening or last KYC updation date [S2].

A commercial bank must obtain any two of the listed documents or their equivalent e-documents as proof of business/activity for a proprietary firm [S1]. The list includes items such as a Registration certificate including Udyam Registration Certificate (URC) and Sales and income tax returns [S1].
The bank shall not require CDD of all the members of an SHG while opening the savings bank account of the SHG [S1]. The CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice [S1].

A commercial bank shall categorise customers into low, medium, and high-risk categories based on its assessment and risk perception [S1]. The bank may also lay down broad principles for the risk-categorisation of customers [S1].

The provided passages do not specify how often a commercial bank must re-check the risk ratings assigned to customer accounts under the RBI's KYC Directions. [S1], [S4] detail periodic updation frequencies based on risk category (two years for high-risk, eight for medium-risk, and ten for low-risk) for Commercial Banks and Payments Banks, respectively. [S3] requires a periodic review of risk categorisation of accounts at least once every six months for Commercial Banks.
A bank must disclose full-fledged information on its products and their implications to customers so they can make an informed judgment about their product choice [S1].

All aspects concerning the renewal of overdue term deposits must be laid down in a transparent, non-discretionary, and non-discriminatory policy [S1]. The terms and conditions of renewal, including interest rates, must be notified to the customer when the deposit is accepted [S1].

The provisions of the Commercial Banks - Responsible Business Conduct Directions shall be in addition to, and not in derogation of the provisions of any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions, for the time being in force [S5]. However, existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines relating to Responsible Business Conduct for Commercial Banks were repealed vide circular DOR.RRC.REC.302/33-01-010/2025-26 dated November 28, 2025 [S1].

Printed material used by retail customers, including account opening forms, pay-in-slips, and passbooks, must be available in trilingual form: English, Hindi, and the concerned Regional Language [S1].

A commercial bank must ensure necessary infrastructure and facilities are in place and appropriate security measures are taken in each branch where loans are sanctioned against gold and/or silver collateral [S1]. Furthermore, the collateral must only be handled in its branches and only by its employees [S1]. The bank shall store the collateral only in branches manned by its employees and having safe deposit vaults fit for storing gold and silver [S3].

A bank shall be guided by Reserve Bank’s instructions on interest rates on deposit accounts and related matters as prescribed in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 [S1]. These Directions are called the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Interest Rate on Deposits) Directions, 2025 [S2].
NOT FOUND

A commercial bank should periodically organise Exporters' Meet at centres with concentration of exporters [S1]. Additionally, a bank should open Export Counsel Offices to guide exporters, especially small ones and those involved in non-traditional exports [S2].

The policy must cover the auction procedure, specifying the trigger event for the auction of eligible collateral and the timeline for serving an auction notice upon the borrower [S1]. It must also cover the mode of auction and the notice period allowed to the borrower(s) / legal heir(s) for loan settlement before auction [S1].

A bank may provide additional facilities beyond the minimum in a BSBD account, with or without charges, provided it is done in a non-discretionary and non-discriminatory manner with transparent disclosure [S1]. However, the bank shall not require the customer to maintain a minimum balance for these additional facilities, and their availment is at the customer's option [S1].

A bank shall undertake at least an annual review for accounts where there is no customer-induced transaction for more than a year [S1]. For term deposits without an explicit renewal mandate, the bank must review them if customers have not withdrawn proceeds or transferred them to savings/current accounts to prevent them from becoming unclaimed [S1].

Warnings can be displayed in bank branches in the official language of the state, and the bank may also consider places like ATMs or Business Correspondent Points for wider visibility [S1]. Additionally, the bank may design suitable posters, pamphlets, flyers, or notices containing messages cautioning against dubious schemes [S3].

Yes, the bank, as principal, is responsible for the actions of its agents [S1]. The bank shall ensure that its agents engaged for recovery of its dues strictly adhere to the instructions while engaged in the process of recovery of dues [S1].

A bank shall have "Enquiry" or "May I Help You" counters either exclusively or combined with other duties, located near the entry point of the banking hall, at all branches excluding very small branches [S1].
The prescribed post-shipment interest rate will cease from the date of credit to the 'Nostro' account [S1].

The bank shall undertake special drives periodically to find out the whereabouts of the customers, their nominees or legal heirs in respect of inoperative accounts / unclaimed deposits [S1]. Additionally, the bank shall contact the holder(s) through letters, email, or SMS on a quarterly basis if the email and mobile number are registered [S4]. If the whereabouts are not traceable, the bank must contact the introducer, if any, and the registered nominee [S3].

A bank must conduct regular audits of service providers, including subcontractors, [S1]. These audits may be performed by the bank's internal or external auditors appointed on the bank's behalf [S1]. The audits shall assess the service provider's performance, risk management practices, and compliance with laws and regulations [S3].
The selection of a group entity shall be based on objective reasons that are similar to the selection of a third-party [S1].

The NBFC shall be responsible for the actions of its service provider, including Direct Sales Agents (DSAs) / Direct Marketing Agents (DMAs) and recovery agents [S1]. Similarly, a bank shall be responsible for the actions of its service provider, including DSAs / DMAs and recovery agents [S2].

No, a commercial bank shall ensure that the service provider, if not a group company, shall not be owned or controlled by any director, or key managerial personnel, or approver of the outsourcing arrangement of the bank, or their relatives [S1]. An exception to this requirement may be made with the approval of the Board or a Committee of the Board, followed by appropriate disclosure, oversight and monitoring [S1].

It suffices if there is clear separation and isolation of data (bank, and its customer specific data and information) to ensure that only personnel authorized by the bank can access data belonging to them in a multi-tenant environment/architecture [S1].

Outsourcing arrangements entered into by a bank shall not affect the rights of its customers against the bank, including the ability of the customers to obtain redressal as applicable under relevant laws [S2]. Furthermore, the responsibility for redressal of customers’ grievances related to outsourced services shall rest with the bank [S3].

A commercial bank's agreement should include the bank's right to conduct audits on the service provider, whether by its internal or external auditors, or by agents appointed to act on its behalf, and to obtain copies of any audit or review reports and findings [S2]. Furthermore, a bank shall conduct regular audits of service providers, including subcontractors, which may be done by the bank's internal or external auditors appointed on the bank's behalf [S4].

A bank may outsource any IT service within its business group or conglomerate provided the arrangement is backed by a Board-approved policy and appropriate SLAs/agreements with its group entities are in place [S1]. In a group structure, a bank may have back-office and service arrangements or agreements with group entities, including outsourcing certain financial services to other group entities [S5].

Yes, a commercial bank may adopt a pooled (shared) audit with other REs if multiple REs are availing services from the same third-party service provider [S1]. This allows the relevant REs to either pool their audit resources or engage an independent third-party auditor to jointly audit the common service provider [S1]. However, the REs remain responsible for ensuring their respective contract audit requirements are met effectively [S1].

When evaluating a service provider for outsourced IT services, a commercial bank must consider technology, infrastructural stability, data backup arrangements, and disaster recovery plan, along with conflict of interest [S1]. Additional considerations include the capability to identify and segregate the bank's data, and the ability to comply with regulatory and legal requirements [S1]. Furthermore, the bank must assess information/cyber security risk and ensure appropriate controls for data protection and bank access to processed data [S1].

A bank shall create an inventory of IT services outsourced to service providers, including key entities involved in their supply chains [S1]. Furthermore, a bank shall map its dependency on third parties and periodically evaluate the information received from the service providers [S1].

A commercial bank must consider the availability of alternative service providers or the possibility of bringing the outsourced activity back in-house in an emergency, along with the associated costs, time, and resources [S1]. Furthermore, contingency plans must ensure business continuity [S4]. Senior Management must ensure that contingency plans, based on realistic and probable disruptive scenarios, are in place and tested [S5].

The Board, or a Committee of the Board to which powers have been delegated, is responsible for approving a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements [S2]. Additionally, the Board or a Committee of the Board shall be responsible for putting in place a framework to evaluate the risks and materiality of all existing and prospective outsourcing arrangements [S1].

Yes, the provisions apply to subcontracted activities [S1]. Before a service provider engages any subcontractor for all or part of the outsourced activity, the outsourcing contract must provide for the prior approval or consent of the bank [S1]. The bank must review the subcontracting arrangement to ensure it complies with the Directions set out in Chapter III [S1].

Commercial banks are prohibited from outsourcing core management functions such as Internal Audit, the compliance function, and decision-making functions like determining compliance with KYC norms for opening deposit accounts, giving sanction for loans (including retail loans), and management of investment portfolio [S1].

A bank must put in place a risk management framework that comprehensively deals with the processes and responsibilities for identification, measurement, mitigation, management, and reporting of risks associated with IT outsourcing arrangements [S1]. Additionally, a bank shall have a management structure to monitor and control its outsourced services, which includes monitoring performance, uptime, service availability, adherence to SLA requirements, and incident response mechanism [S2].

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Credit Cards and Debit Cards: Issuance and Conduct) Directions, 2025 are applicable to Commercial Banks [S3]. For this purpose, 'Commercial Banks' include banking companies (excluding Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks), corresponding new banks, and the State Bank of India [S3].

Card-issuers must ensure that their call centre staff are trained adequately to competently handle and escalate a complaint if necessary [S1], [S2]. The Grievance Redressal process must include a provision for automatic escalation of unresolved complaints from a call center/base level to higher authorities [S1], [S2].

The co-branded card must explicitly indicate that it has been issued under a cobranding arrangement [S1]. Additionally, in all marketing/advertising material, the name of the card-issuer shall be clearly shown [S1].

Card-issuers and their agents shall not resort to intimidation or harassment of any kind, either verbal or physical, during debt collection efforts, including public humiliation or intruding upon the privacy of family members, referees, and friends, or making threatening/anonymous calls or false/misleading representations [S3]. Furthermore, card-issuers must ensure agents refrain from actions damaging integrity and reputation and observe strict customer confidentiality [S1].

Prior approval of the Reserve Bank is not necessary for the issuance of co-branded debit cards, co-branded prepaid cards, and co-branded credit cards for Commercial Banks, subject to stipulated conditions [S1]. Additionally, prior approval is not necessary for banks issuing debit cards to their customers [S3].

If no OTP-based consent is received for activating a credit card that has not been activated for more than 30 days from the date of issuance, the card-issuer shall close the credit card account without any cost to the customer within seven working days from the date of seeking confirmation from the customer [S1]. This requirement is also stated for Commercial Banks [S1].

The monetary threshold that triggers the requirement for explicit consent is one percent of the credit limit or ₹5000, whichever is lower [S1]. This applies to credit amounts beyond this cut-off arising from refund, failed, or reversed transactions against the credit limit for which payment has already been made by the cardholder [S1].

The card-issuer must explicitly bring to the notice of the customer that the information relating to the credit history or repayment record is being provided in terms of the Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005 [S1]. This requirement also applies to Non-Banking Financial Companies [S2].

All communications issued by recovery agents must contain the name, email-id, telephone number, and address of the concerned senior officer of the card-issuer whom the customer can contact [S1]. Similarly, for Non-Banking Financial Companies, all communications issued by recovery agents must contain the name, email-id, telephone number, and address of the concerned senior officer of the card-issuer whom the customer can contact [S2].

A bank shall report a credit card account as ‘past due’ to credit information companies (CICs) or levy penal charges only when a credit card account remains overdue for more than three days [S2]. Similarly, card-issuers shall report a credit card account as 'past due' or levy penal charges only when it remains 'past due' for more than three days [S1].

Card-issuers shall not levy any charge that was not explicitly indicated to the cardholders at the time of issue of the card and without getting their explicit consent [S1]. This rule does not apply to charges like service taxes levied by the Government or any other statutory authority [S1].

Yes, card-issuers may issue business credit cards to individuals for business expenses [S2]. Business Credit Cards are issued to business entities or individuals for the purpose of business expenses with specified terms and conditions and not for personal use [S3].

Each card-issuer must have a well-documented policy for the issuance and conduct of credit cards, approved by its Board or a delegated Committee [S1]. This policy must be in consonance with instructions issued by the Reserve Bank and these Directions, and it must be available on the card-issuer's website [S1].

Card-issuers, which includes commercial banks, shall ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to cardholders [S1]. Similarly, for Non-Banking Financial Companies, card-issuers must ensure that wrong bills are not raised and issued to cardholders [S2].

Card-issuers must make available to cardholders in writing a set of contractual terms and conditions governing the issue and use of such cards [S4]. These terms must be expressed clearly and maintain a fair balance between the interests of the parties concerned [S4].

The disclosure of customers’ information to DSAs, DMAs, or recovery agents shall be limited to the extent that will enable them to discharge their duties [S1]. Personal information provided by the cardholder but not required for recovery purposes shall not be released by the card-issuer [S1].

A bank shall have the freedom to determine interest on deposits of money accepted or renewed under the RFC Account Scheme, in accordance with a comprehensive policy duly approved by the Board of Directors or a delegated Committee [S1]. Interest rates on NRE/NRO deposits shall not be higher than those offered on comparable domestic rupee term deposits [S2].

If a term deposit is withdrawn before the maturity date, interest shall be paid at the rate applicable to the amount and period for which the deposit remained with the bank and not at the contracted rate [S1]. However, no interest shall be paid if the premature withdrawal occurs before the minimum period specified in paragraph 10(1) [S1].
The minimum tenor for NRE term deposits is one year, and for NRO term deposits, it is seven days [S1].

Rupee deposits of non-residents under NRE and NRO must only be accepted by banks authorized under the Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999 (FEMA) by the Reserve Bank of India from time to time [S1]. A bank must also have a comprehensive policy approved by the Board of Directors or a delegated Committee regarding interest rates on deposits [S2].

A bank may, at its discretion, allow an additional interest of one per cent per annum over and above the rate mentioned in the schedule of interest rates on savings or term deposits to its staff and their exclusive associations [S1]. This additional interest is payable until the person remains eligible or until the maturity of a term deposit account [S1].
If the claimants of an NRE term deposit account of a deceased depositor are residents, the deposit on maturity shall be treated as a domestic rupee term deposit [S1].

The rate of interest on matured deposits for a deceased individual depositor or two or more joint depositors where one has died shall be as per the comprehensive policy on interest rate on deposits and subject to the conditions in paragraph 7 of these Directions [S2].

If the components of penalty for premature withdrawal of FCNR(B) term deposits are not clearly brought to the notice of the depositors at the time of acceptance, the exchange loss arising out of premature withdrawal shall be borne by the bank [S1].

If the period from the date of maturity till the date of renewal does not exceed 14 days, the interest rate payable on the renewed FCNR(B) deposit shall be the appropriate rate prevailing on the date of maturity or on the date the depositor seeks renewal, whichever is lower [S1].

Any action taken or purported to have been taken, or initiated under the repealed Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof [S1]. All approvals or acknowledgments granted under these repealed lists shall be deemed as governed by these Directions [S1].

No penalty for premature withdrawal of a term deposit shall be levied if the period and aggregate amount of the deposit do not change when the amount is split at the request of claimant(s) of deceased depositors or joint account holders [S1], [S2]. Additionally, no penalty for premature withdrawal shall be levied where depositors of a specific branch desire premature withdrawal consequent to the transfer of business to another bank [S2], [S3], [S5].

Yes, a bank may, at its discretion, give its resident Indian retired staff who are senior citizens the benefit of additional interest rates as admissible to senior citizens over and above the additional interest payable to them by virtue of being retired members of the bank’s staff [S1].

Interest on the minimum credit balance in the composite cash credit account of a farmer is paid for the period from the 10th to the last day of each calendar month [S1]. The composite cash credit is a loan product with a cash credit limit and a fully savings module designed for the farmer's interest [S5].

A comprehensive policy approved by the Board of Directors or a delegated Committee must cover the interest rate on deposits and penalties for premature withdrawal of term deposits, including partial premature withdrawal [S3]. Specifically, this policy must address penalties for premature withdrawal of NRE term deposits and FCNR(B) term deposits [S3].

A bank shall pay interest when converting an FCNR(B) Account into an RFC / Resident Rupee Account even if the minimum maturity period has not been completed, subject to conditions in paragraph 7 [S1]. The rate of interest shall not exceed the rate payable on savings bank deposits held under RFC Account Scheme [S1].

A commercial bank may use foreign currency funds borrowed under Notification No. FEMA.3(R)/2018-RB dated December 17, 2018, or foreign currency funds generated through buy-sell swaps in the domestic forex market for granting PCFC [S3]. Additionally, foreign currency balances in Exchange Earners Foreign Currency (EEFC) Accounts, Resident Foreign Currency Accounts RFC(D), and Foreign Currency (Non-Resident) Accounts (Banks) Scheme may be utilized for financing PCFC [S4].

The bank must ensure that the final products are exported by the processors/exporters according to the terms and conditions of the sanction to liquidate the pre-shipment credit as per extant instructions [S1]. Rupee pre-shipment and post-shipment export credit can be extended to parties against orders for supplies in projects aided/financed by bilateral or multilateral agencies/funds, as notified by the Department of Economic Affairs, Ministry of Finance [S2].

The exposure of a bank by way of PCEs to bonds issued by each such NBFC / HFC shall be restricted to one per cent of capital funds of the RE within the extant single / group borrower exposure limits [S1]. Additionally, the PCE exposure limit by a single NBFC shall be 50 per cent of the bond issue size [S2].

All corporates and other constituent borrowers with a turnover above a threshold level fixed by the bank’s Board of Directors must disclose the ‘aging schedule’ of their overdue payables in their periodical returns submitted to banks to promote payment discipline [S1]. NOT FOUND

A bank shall grant export credit to exporters with a good track record until the realization of proceeds from a cheque or draft received from abroad, provided it is against an export order, aligns with trade practices, and is an approved method of realization of export proceeds as per extant rules [S1].

When introducing any kind of product, a commercial bank must take into account the customer suitability and appropriateness [S1]. Furthermore, the bank must ensure that borrowers/customers are fully aware of the risks and liabilities under such products [S1].

The bank must ensure that borrowers obtain prior permission from government, local governments, or other statutory authorities for the project, wherever required [S2]. Disbursements shall only be made after the borrower has obtained requisite clearances from the government authorities, even if the proposals were sanctioned normally [S2]. Additionally, the bank must ensure compliance with terms stipulating that the builder/developer discloses the mortgaging bank's name in pamphlets/brochures and appends mortgage information in advertisements, and that the builder/developer will provide an NOC/permission of the mortgagee bank for sale if required, before releasing funds [S1].

The builder/developer/company must disclose in the Pamphlets/Brochures etc., the name(s) of the bank(s) to which the property is mortgaged [S1]. Additionally, they must indicate in their pamphlets/brochures that they shall provide a No Objection Certificate (NOC) / permission of the mortgagee bank for the sale of flats/property, if required [S1].

A bank shall not enter into a leasing agreement with another equipment leasing company and other non-banking finance company engaged in equipment leasing [S2]. Furthermore, banks shall not enter into lease agreements departmentally with equipment leasing companies or other NBFCs engaged in equipment leasing [S1].

Bills rediscounted 'with recourse' in the domestic market should only be reflected in the case of the first bank discounting the bills, as that bank alone will have recourse to the exporter [S1]. The bank rediscounting shall not reckon this amount as export credit [S1].

The value of gold or silver accepted as collateral shall be based on the reference price corresponding to its actual purity [S1]. This reference price is the lower of the average closing price over the preceding 30 days or the closing price on the preceding day, as published by IBJA or a SEBI-regulated commodity exchange [S1]. For valuation, only the intrinsic value of the gold or silver contained in the eligible collateral shall be reckoned, excluding other cost elements like precious stones or gems [S4].

A microfinance loan is defined as a collateral-free loan given to a household with an annual household income up to ₹3,00,000 [S1]. All collateral-free loans provided to low-income households, meaning those with an annual income up to ₹3,00,000, are considered microfinance loans [S2]. The loan must not be linked with a lien on the borrower's deposit account or backed by hypothecation of any security [S2].

A commercial bank must capture and maintain project-specific data in an electronic and easily accessible format on an ongoing basis [S2]. The minimum parameters for this database include Debtor Profile, Original Project Profile, and Change in DCCO [S2].

No, the bank shall not grant finance for the construction of buildings meant purely for Government / Semi-Government offices, including Municipal and Panchayat offices [S1]. However, the bank may grant loans for activities related to such construction if those activities will be refinanced by institutions like NABARD [S1].

A bank shall accept DLG in one or more of the following forms: cash deposited with the bank, a Fixed Deposit maintained with a Scheduled Commercial Bank with a lien marked in favour of the bank, or a Bank Guarantee in favour of the bank [S1].

An Internet Banking Channel is a digital banking channel offered over the internet, including web browser-based applications but excluding mobile applications [S1]. A Mobile Banking Channel is a digital banking channel offered using mobile applications, USSD, and SMS [S1].

Yes, the Reserve Bank may grant an extension of time to comply with or exempt any regulated entity from all or any provisions of the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, if it considers necessary for avoiding hardship or for any other just and sufficient reason [S1]. This exemption can be granted generally or for a specified period, subject to conditions imposed by the Reserve Bank [S1].

Commercial banks must adhere to the provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and other legal requirements [S1]. Additionally, they must comply with FEMA 1999 and applicable instructions issued by the Reserve Bank [S1]. The jurisdiction for legal settlement within India is specified [S1].

Banks must require prior approval of the Reserve Bank for launching a transactional banking facility [S1]. Subject to fulfilling eligibility criteria, banks may apply to the Department of Regulation, Reserve Bank of India through the PRAVAAH portal [S1].

Yes, banks shall obtain explicit consent from the customer for registering for digital banking services, and this consent must be duly recorded/documented [S1]. Furthermore, it must be clearly indicated that SMS/email alerts will be sent to the customer's registered mobile number/email for both financial and non-financial operations [S1].

The interpretation of any provision of the Directions by the RBI shall be final and binding on all concerned entities [S2]. This is also stated for the Digital Banking Channels Authorisation Directions, 2025, where the interpretation given by the RBI shall be final and binding [S1].

A commercial bank must follow the guidelines specified in the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Managing Risks in Outsourcing) Directions, 2025 when adopting an outsourced model for the digital banking segment [S2]. Additionally, all banks offering digital banking services must comply with several specific instructions, including the Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices and the Master Direction on Digital Payment Security Controls [S1].

All banks must have implemented Core Banking Solution (CBS) and enabled their public facing Information technology (IT) infrastructure to handle Internet Protocol Version 6 (IPv6) traffic to be eligible to provide view only banking facility for internet banking, mobile banking, and other digital banking channels-based services [S1]. A view only banking facility only allows services that do not alter the asset or liability of the customer, such as balance enquiry or account statement download [S2].

Banks must put in place comprehensive policy(ies) for all digital banking channels, taking into account all statutory and regulatory requirements, including the management of liquidity and operational risks in a digital banking scenario [S1]. Additionally, banks must ensure continuous adherence to various provisions such as the Information Technology Act, 2000, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and instructions from the Reserve Bank of India [S4].

Yes, the provisions of the Directions are in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions currently in force [S5]. Furthermore, banks must ensure continuous adherence to the provisions of the Information Technology Act, 2000, Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023, and other legal requirements in their digital banking operations [S1].

The Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Digital Banking Channels Authorisation) Directions, 2025 are applicable to Commercial Banks [S5]. For the purpose of these Directions, 'Commercial Banks' mean banking companies other than Small Finance Banks, Payment Banks, and Local Area Banks, corresponding new banks, and the State Bank of India [S5]. All banks offering digital banking services must comply with the Directions in this chapter continuously [S1].

The bank shall consider lodging a formal complaint against the statutory auditors with the National Financial Reporting Authority (NFRA) / Institute of Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI) [S1]. Pending disciplinary action, the complaints must be forwarded to the Reserve Bank (Department of Supervision, Central Office) and Indian Banks' Association (IBA) after the bank satisfies itself of the auditors' involvement and provides them an opportunity to be heard [S1].

The responsibility for reporting correct information and ensuring the accuracy of facts and figures rests with the reporting bank [S2]. When furnishing information to credit information companies, a bank must also ensure the accuracy of the particulars of the directors, cross-checking with the Registrar of Companies database where possible [S2].

The bar on additional credit facility to a wilful defaulter or any associated entity shall be effective for a period of one year after the name of the wilful defaulter has been removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters by the lenders [S1]. Additionally, no credit facility shall be granted by the bank for floating of new ventures to the wilful defaulter or any associated entity for a period of five years after the name has been removed from the List of Wilful Defaulters by the lenders [S2].

The name of a borrower or guarantor classified as a wilful defaulter shall be removed from the LWD after implementation of the resolution plan under IBC or the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks – Resolution of Stressed Assets) Directions, 2025, if the account was in LWD and subsequently underwent liquidation or the resolution resulted in a change in the management and control of the entity/business enterprise [S1].

A commercial bank shall put in place a transparent mechanism for the entire process of identification of wilful defaulters so that the penal provisions are applied in a fair manner and the scope for discretion is obviated [S1]. The objective of these Directions is to provide for a non-discriminatory and transparent procedure, having regard to the principles of natural justice, for classifying a borrower as a wilful defaulter by banks [S3].

A commercial bank must submit information regarding wilful defaulters at monthly intervals [S1]. This information includes a list of wilful defaulters (LWD) for suit filed accounts and a LWD for non-suit filed accounts [S1].

Before transferring a defaulted loan with an outstanding of ₹25 lakh and above, a commercial bank must internally conduct a comprehensive investigation from a wilful default perspective [S1]. This process need not necessarily involve a two-stage committee but must ensure a thorough examination of wilful default aspects for each defaulted loan [S1].

A commercial bank should forward the details of these third parties to the Indian Banks' Association (IBA) for records, regardless of the bank's membership status with the IBA [S1]. Before reporting to IBA, the bank must satisfy itself of the concerned third parties' involvement and provide them with an opportunity to be heard, following a suitably recorded due process [S1].

When a default occurs in payment or repayment by the principal debtor, a bank can proceed against the guarantor even without exhausting the remedies against the principal debtor [S1]. The liability of the guarantor is immediate once the bank makes a claim on them due to the principal debtor's default [S1].

Standard assets provisioning for microfinance loans of an NBFC-MFI lying in a particular layer of the scale based regulatory framework must be in accordance with instructions contained in Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 for the respective layer [S2].

Loans disbursed or managed by an NBFC-MFI in its capacity as a channelizing agent for Central or State Government Agencies shall be considered a separate business segment [S1]. These loans should not be included in the numerator (microfinance loans) or the denominator (total assets) when determining compliance with the minimum threshold of microfinance loans [S1].

An NBFC-MFI must adhere to the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 regarding the treatment of deferred tax assets and deferred tax liabilities for capital computation [S1]. Specifically, certain Deferred Tax Assets (DTAs) must be deducted in full from CET1 capital, including those associated with accumulated losses and DTAs (excluding those associated with accumulated losses) net of DTL [S2].

The treatment to on-balance and off-balance sheet assets for capital adequacy shall be as provided in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025 [S4]. For computing Risk-Weighted Assets (RWAs), risk-weights for on-balance sheet items are provided in a table, and the aggregate of the risk-adjusted value of on-balance sheet assets is used for reckoning the minimum capital ratio [S2].

An NBFC-MFI shall adhere to the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 [S4]. Additionally, an NBFC-MFI must adhere to the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Risk Management) Directions, 2025 [S2]. Furthermore, an NBFC-MFI must adhere to the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Credit Facilities) Directions, 2025 as part of the directions on credit facilities and various financial services [S3].
An NBFC-MFI shall adhere to the provisions of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Asset Liability Management) Directions, 2025 [S5].

The provisions of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 apply to NBFC-Micro Finance Institutions registered with the RBI under the RBI Act, 1934, unless they conflict with the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Microfinance Institution) Directions, 2025 [S2]. Standard assets provisioning for microfinance loans of an NBFC-MFI must follow instructions in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Income Recognition, Asset Classification and Provisioning) Directions, 2025 for the respective layer [S3].

An NBFC-MFI shall adhere to the provisions of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025 [S2]. Additionally, an NBFC-MFI must adhere to paragraphs 10, 11, 13, 14 and 15 of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Branch Authorisation) Directions, 2025 regarding opening a branch or representative office abroad and closure of branches [S5].
An NBFC that does not qualify as an NBFC-MFI shall extend microfinance loans that in aggregate do not exceed 25 per cent of its total assets [S1].

Standard asset is an asset where no default in repayment of principal or payment of interest is perceived, and it does not disclose any problem nor carry more than normal risk attached to the business [S2].

An NBFC-MFI shall maintain a capital adequacy ratio consisting of Tier 1 and Tier 2 capital which shall not be less than 15 per cent of its aggregate risk weighted assets of on-balance sheet and of risk adjusted value of off-balance sheet items [S1]. NBFC-MFI shall refer to the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Prudential Norms on Capital Adequacy) Directions, 2025, for minimum applicable regulatory capital requirements [S2].

The Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Microfinance Institution) Directions, 2025 are applicable to every Non-Banking Financial Company – Microfinance Institution registered with the Reserve Bank under the provisions of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 [S2]. The passages do not state that other RBI directions apply to every NBFC-MFI in the same way; for instance, the NBFC-MFI Directions, 2025 are specifically applicable to NBFC-MFI registered under the RBI Act, 1934 [S5].

Any action taken or purported to have been taken, or initiated under the repealed Directions, instructions, or guidelines shall continue to be governed by the provisions thereof [S1]. Furthermore, any right, obligation, or liability acquired, accrued, or incurred thereunder shall not be prejudicially affected by the repeal [S1]. The existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines applicable to Non-Banking Financial Companies- Microfinance Institutions stand repealed as of November 28, 2025 [S2].

The provided passages do not specify a deadline for quarterly regulatory statements from an NBFC lender participating in a P2P platform. [S1], [S3], and [S5] detail requirements for NBFC-P2P, but none address the submission timeline for a lender's quarterly statements to the RBI Regional Office.
An NBFC-P2P shall comply with the Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices dated November 07, 2023 (as amended from time to time) [S1].

The Board of Directors must provide for a periodical review of the compliance of the Fair Practices Code and the functioning of the grievance redressal mechanism at various levels of management, with a consolidated report submitted to the Board at regular intervals [S1]. Additionally, the Board must ensure that an NBFC has Board approved policies and review mechanisms to ensure responsible business conduct, which includes a Fair Practices Code and a grievance redressal mechanism [S3]. For NBFC-P2P, the Board must establish periodic review mechanisms to ensure sound processes and systems, including the Fair Practices Code and Participant Grievance Redressal Mechanism [S2].

An NBFC-P2P must maintain at least two escrow accounts: one for funds received from lenders and pending disbursal (Lenders’ escrow Account), and another for collections from borrowers (Borrowers’ escrow Account) [S1]. Funds from the lenders’ bank accounts are transferred only to the Lenders’ Escrow Account, and funds from the Borrowers’ Escrow Account are used only for transferring to the respective lender’s bank account [S1].

An allotment of shares for an NBFC-P2P requires the Reserve Bank's prior written permission if it will take the aggregate holding of an individual or group to equivalent of 26 per cent and more of the paid-up capital of the NBFC-P2P [S2].

An Information System Audit of the internal systems and processes for an NBFC-P2P shall be conducted at least once in two years by CISA certified external auditors [S1]. The report must be submitted to the Regional Office of the Department of Supervision of the Reserve Bank within one month of the external auditor's submission [S1].

An NBFC-P2P may make use of the ‘Guidance Note on Operational Risk Management and Operational Resilience’, as amended from time to time [S2]. Additionally, an NBFC-P2P shall comply with Master Direction on Information Technology Governance, Risk, Controls and Assurance Practices dated November 07, 2023 (as amended from time to time) [S1].

Yes, the instructions in these Directions shall be applicable to an NBFC-P2P in addition and not in substitution to the other relevant instructions contained in the directions mentioned in paragraph 4 [S2].

Yes, the Reserve Bank may grant in-principle approval subject to such conditions which it may consider fit to impose after being satisfied that the conditions in paragraph 15 are fulfilled [S2]. Furthermore, the Reserve Bank may grant a CoR subject to conditions as deemed fit by the Reserve Bank [S4].

An NBFC-P2P must comply with the relevant instructions in the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Credit Information Reporting) Directions, 2025 for reporting and updating credit information related to borrower transactions [S1]. For this purpose, the NBFC-P2P must include necessary consents in the agreement with participants for providing the credit information [S1].
The Leverage Ratio for an NBFC-P2P is calculated as the Total Outside Liabilities divided by Owned Funds [S2]. An NBFC-P2P shall maintain a Leverage Ratio not exceeding two [S1].

No, an NBFC-P2P shall not hold on its own balance sheet funds received from lenders for lending [S1]. This also includes funds received from borrowers for servicing loans, or funds stipulated in paragraphs 37 and 38 of the Directions [S1].

The provisions of the Directions are in addition to, and not in derogation of, any other laws, rules, regulations, or directions in force [S1]. The instructions in these Directions are applicable to an NBFC-P2P in addition and not in substitution to the other relevant instructions mentioned in paragraph 4 [S5]. Existing Directions, instructions, and guidelines relating to Non-Banking Financial Companies – Peer to Peer Lending Platforms are repealed with the issue of these Directions [S2].

An NBFC-P2P shall communicate changes of address, directors, and auditors as prescribed in paragraphs 6 and 7 of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 [S1]. Additionally, an NBFC-P2P must advise the Reserve Bank of any change of Directors or key management personnel [S2].

An NBFC-P2P must comply with the provisions of paragraphs 6(1) and 6(2) of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025 [S2]. Furthermore, prior written permission from the Reserve Bank is required for any share allotment that brings an individual or group's aggregate holding to 26 percent or more of the paid-up capital of the NBFC-P2P, or for any change in shareholding that grants the acquirer the right to nominate a Director [S2]. An NBFC-P2P must comply with the instructions in paragraph 7 of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Acquisition of Shareholding or Control) Directions, 2025, regarding prior approval for these requirements [S3].

An NBFC-P2P shall put in place a Fair Practices Code based on the Guidelines outlined herein, with the approval of its Board [S1]. Additionally, the NBFC-P2P shall put in place Board approved policies, which include a Fair Practices Code [S2].

An NBFC-AA shall form a Nomination Committee consisting of not less than three members of its Board of Directors [S1]. This committee is required to ensure the 'fit and proper' status of proposed or existing directors [S1].

NBFC-AA shall comply with the disclosure requirements specified in Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Financial Statements: Presentation and Disclosures) Directions, 2025, except for provisions in paragraphs 13 to 15 and paragraph 20 [S1]. These disclosures are in addition to and not in substitution of requirements under other laws, regulations, or accounting and financial reporting standards [S1].

An NBFC-AA shall communicate changes regarding address, directors, and auditors, as prescribed in paragraphs 6 and 7 of Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies – Miscellaneous) Directions, 2025 [S2].

The Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Account Aggregator) Directions, 2025 apply to every non-banking financial company undertaking the business of Account Aggregator [S4]. Specifically, the NBFC-Account Aggregator (NBFC-AA) consolidates financial information held by a customer across different financial entities [S2].

The instructions in the NBFC-Account Aggregator Directions are applicable to an NBFC-AA in addition to, and not in substitution to, the other relevant instructions contained in the directions mentioned in paragraph 4 above [S1].

The interpretation of any provision of the Reserve Bank of India (Non-Banking Financial Companies - Account Aggregator) Directions, 2025, is final and binding, as stated in paragraph 64 [S1]. The Reserve Bank of India issues these Directions in exercise of powers conferred under section 45JA of the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934 [S2].

No, an NBFC-AA or the Financial Information User shall not use or disclose financial information except as specified in the consent artefact [S1]. Furthermore, an NBFC-AA shall not use or access customer information other than for performing the business explicitly requested by the customer [S4].

The NBFC-AA must verify the identity of the Financial Information User [S1]. If verified, the NBFC-AA shall securely transfer the customer’s information to the intended recipient in accordance with the terms of the consent artefact [S1].

An NBFC-AA must have a Board approved policy for pricing of services [S1]. This pricing must conform strictly with the internal guidelines adopted by the NBFC-AA, which need to be transparent and available in the public domain [S1]. Additionally, the NBFC-AA shall put in place Board approved policies, including one for Pricing of Services [S2].
NBFC-AA shall always remain in the Base Layer of the regulatory structure [S2].
The NBFC-AA is responsible for ensuring its IT systems have all necessary features to strictly conform with the Directions as updated from time to time [S2].

A standardized consent artefact obtained by the NBFC-AA must include the customer's identity and optional contact information, the nature and purpose of the financial information requested, the identity of recipients, a notification URL, consent creation and expiry dates, and the NBFC-AA's identity and signature/digital signature [S1]. The NBFC-AA must inform the customer of all necessary attributes for the consent artefact and the right to file complaints [S2].

No financial information of the customer shall be retrieved, shared or transferred by the NBFC-AA without the explicit consent of the customer [S5].

This requirement also applies to Non-Banking Financial Companies [S1].

The Technical Working Group (TWG) shall review the data reporting formats at least once a year [S1]. If any recommendations are made, they shall be made to the Reserve Bank [S1].

The Standing Sub-Group of TWG is an advisory and collaborative body to offer expert insights and make recommendations on technical aspects of credit information reporting [S2]. Its purpose is to support in-depth discussions regarding challenges encountered by CIs and CICs in relation to credit information reporting, including necessary modifications to IT systems in data reporting formats [S2].
For the microfinance segment, the required format is Form 3: Uniform Credit Reporting Format (MFI) [S1, S3].

NBFCs covered under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme, 2021 (RBIOS, 2021) shall comply with the directions provided under the said Scheme [S2]. Additionally, NBFCs covered under RBIOS, 2021 shall comply with the directions provided under the said Scheme [S3]. A CI covered under the Reserve Bank – Integrated Ombudsman Scheme (RB-IOS), as amended from time to time, shall comply with the directions provided under the said Scheme [S1].
Meetings of the TWG shall be held at least once in a calendar year [S3].

The TWG for Non-Banking Financial Companies includes representatives from Public Sector Banks, Private Sector Banks, Foreign Banks, Primary (Urban) Cooperative Banks (UCBs), Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), All India Notified Financial Institutions (AIFIs), Non-Banking Financial Companies (NBFCs), Housing Finance Companies (HFCs), Asset Reconstruction Companies (ARCs), India Banks’ Association (IBA), Micro Finance Institutions Network (MFIN), Sa-Dhan, and CICs [S1].

PAN or equivalent e-document thereof of customers must be obtained and verified while undertaking transactions as per the provisions of Income Tax Rule 114B applicable to ARCs [S1]. Form 60 must be obtained from persons who do not have PAN or equivalent e-document thereof [S1].

If an existing KYC-compliant customer of an ARC desires to open another account or avail of any other product or service from the same ARC, there shall be no need for a fresh CDD exercise as far as identification of the customer is concerned [S1].
The ARC shall register the details of a non-profit organisation customer on the DARPAN Portal of NITI Aayog if they are not registered [S1].

The ARC shall apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of risks [S1]. The ARC shall carry out ‘Money Laundering (ML) and Terrorist Financing (TF) Risk Assessment’ exercises periodically to identify, assess and take effective measures to mitigate its money laundering and terrorist financing risk [S2].

The ARC shall review its risk assessment at least annually [S1]. The Board or a committee of the Board to which the power has been delegated shall determine the periodicity of the risk assessment exercise, in alignment with the outcome of the risk assessment exercise [S1].
The NBFC shall undertake diligence measures and meticulous monitoring to identify accounts which are operated as Money Mules and take appropriate action [S1].

KYC verification done by one branch or office of the NBFC is valid for transferring the account to any other branch or office of the same NBFC, provided the NBFC has completed the full KYC verification and it is not due for periodic updation [S1].

A delay of each day in not reporting a transaction or delay of each day in rectifying a mis-represented transaction beyond the time limit as specified in the Rule shall constitute as a separate violation for an NBFC [S1].

Yes, these directions apply to the branches and majority-owned subsidiaries of an All India Financial Institution (AIFI) located abroad, to the extent they are not contradictory to the local laws in the host country [S1]. If there is a variance in KYC/AML standards between the RBI and host country regulators, the branches/subsidiaries must adopt the more stringent regulation [S1].

The AIFI shall undertake identification of customers when carrying out any international money transfer operations for a person who is not an account holder of the AIFI [S1]. Additionally, the ordering AIFI must ensure that all cross-border wire transfers contain required and accurate originator and beneficiary information [S2].
For opening an account of a trust at a Small Finance Bank, the bank must obtain the certified copies of the Registration certificate and the PAN or Form No.60 of the trust [S1].

The four key elements that an All India Financial Institution's KYC policy must include are Customer Acceptance Policy, Risk Management, Customer Identification Procedures (CIP), and Monitoring of Transactions [S1].
An AIFI must capture the customer’s KYC records and upload them onto CKYCR within 10 days of the commencement of an account-based relationship with the customer [S1].

A rural co-operative bank shall apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of risks [S2]. The bank must also have Board-approved policies, controls, and procedures in this regard [S2]. Furthermore, the bank shall adopt a risk-based approach for periodic updation of KYC [S1].

The 'at par' cheque facility can be utilized for the bank's own use, for KYC compliant account-holders, or for walk-in customers against cash for less than ₹50,000 per individual [S1]. For KYC compliant account-holders, all transactions of ₹50,000 or more must be strictly by debit to the customers’ accounts [S1].

An Urban Co-operative Bank shall apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of risks [S1]. The bank must have Board-approved policies, controls, and procedures in this regard [S1].

All transactions of ₹50,000 or more must be strictly by debit to the customers’ accounts when using the 'at par' cheque facility for KYC compliant account holders [S1]. This requirement is also stated for Rural Co-operative Banks [S2].

A Regional Rural Bank shall apply a Risk Based Approach (RBA) for mitigation and management of the risks identified on its own or through national risk assessment [S2]. The bank must also have Board-approved policies, controls, and procedures regarding this approach [S2].

The aggregate balance of all the deposit accounts of the customer shall not exceed Rupees One Lakh [S1]. If the balance exceeds this threshold, the bank shall cease the account’s operation until it completes the CDD as mentioned at (5) below [S1].

The bank, its directors, officers, and all employees of a Payments Bank must ensure that the fact of maintaining records referred to in rule 3 of the PML (Maintenance of Records) Rules, 2005, and furnishing this information to the Director is confidential [S1]. However, this confidentiality requirement does not prevent sharing information under paragraph 8 of these Directions regarding any analysis of unusual transactions and activities if the bank has performed such an analysis [S1].
A delay of each day in not reporting a transaction to the Director, FIU-IND shall constitute a separate violation [S1].
The bank shall not require CDD of all the members of an SHG while opening the savings bank account of the SHG [S1]. The CDD of all the office bearers shall suffice [S1].

A small finance bank must put in place an adequate screening mechanism, including a Know Your Employee / Staff policy, as part of its personnel recruitment/hiring process [S1]. The bank must also ensure staff dealing with KYC/AML/CFT matters have high integrity, ethical standards, a good understanding of extant standards, effective communication skills, and the ability to keep up with the changing landscape [S1].
